coreIdea: Dividing every logit by a temperature before the softmax decides how sharply a language model prefers its top word.
title: Temperature decides how sure the next word is
dek: A softmax turns scores into chances. Divide the scores by a temperature first, and one number slides the model from greedy to adventurous.

sections.heading: Scores become chances
paragraphs: At each step a language model gives every word a score, a *logit*. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities: `pᵢ = e^(sᵢ) / Σⱼ e^(sⱼ)`.

sections.heading: One knob for sharpness
paragraphs: Sampling code divides every logit by a temperature T first. Drag T below 1 and watch the top word take almost everything. Drag it above 1 and the bars even out.

sections.heading: From greedy to adventurous
paragraphs: Close scores make the knob matter more. With five near-equal logits, T decides whether the model always says the same thing or wanders. As T approaches 0, sampling becomes **greedy decoding**.

figures.title: Temperature sharpens the softmax
figures.caption: Five candidate next words for “The cat sat on the …”. Drag T.
figures.alt: Bar chart of the chance of five next words at temperature 1, with “mat” highest. Lowering T sharpens the bars into one spike on “mat”; raising T flattens them toward equal heights.

figures.title: Close scores, big swings
figures.caption: Five words with nearly equal logits. Small changes in T move a lot of probability.
figures.alt: Bar chart of five next words whose logits differ by less than one, nearly level at temperature 1. Lowering T toward 0.05 hands almost all of the probability to the first word.

takeaway: A softmax only cares about score differences measured against T. Divide by a small T and the top word wins outright; divide by a large T and every word gets a chance.

coreIdea: A hot object cools in proportion to how much hotter it is than the room, so the gap shrinks by the same fraction every minute.
title: Why coffee cools fast, then slowly
dek: The rate of cooling is proportional to the gap to room temperature. That one rule gives an exponential curve and a fixed half-life for the gap.

sections.heading: Heat flows down the gap
paragraphs: A cup at 90 °C in a 20 °C room loses heat quickly. At 25 °C it barely cools. Newton's law of cooling makes this exact: the rate is proportional to the gap, T − Tₐ.

sections.heading: The curve
paragraphs: Solve it and you get `T(t) = Tₐ + (T₀ − Tₐ)·e^(−kt)`. Drag the point along time and watch the drop slow down. Raise k, the cooling constant, and the whole curve falls faster.

sections.heading: A half-life for the gap
paragraphs: The gap halves every `ln 2 / k` minutes, whatever T₀ is. A cup at 90 °C and one at 50 °C take the same time to halve their gaps.

figures.title: Temperature over time
figures.caption: T(t) = Tₐ + (T₀ − Tₐ)·e^(−kt). Drag the point, then change k and T₀.
figures.alt: Line chart of temperature against time from 0 to 60 minutes, falling from 90 °C toward a room temperature of 20 °C, steeply at first and then slowly. Raising k makes the fall steeper.

figures.title: Faster cooling, shorter half-life
figures.caption: The time for the gap to halve, ln 2 / k, against k.
figures.alt: Line chart of the gap's half-life against the cooling constant k from 0.01 to 0.3 per minute: about 69 minutes at k = 0.01, falling steeply and then flattening near 2 minutes at k = 0.3.

takeaway: Cooling is proportional to the gap, so the gap decays exponentially, T(t) = Tₐ + (T₀ − Tₐ)·e^(−kt), and halves every ln 2 / k minutes from any start.
